May I ask the Prime Minister if anything has been done in the way of providing a building for the housing and caring of our war memorials? The matter was up last session. As I explained at the time, Canada has a wonderful collection of war memorials, in fact I think a collection larger and more important than that possessed by any other country. The Prime Minister then said:
Up to the present time we have felt that there were other demands more imperative than the demand for a building for the purpose of housing these works of art. I think, however, we must not lose sight of the fact that the collection is a national possession, a very valuable possession, and one which as speedily as possible should be properly housed.

International Peace-Optional Clause
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I have been much disappointed to find no provision in the estimates for a building for this purpose. The government seems to be able to spend a lot of money for other buildings in Ottawa. It strikes me that a building to house our war memorials is more necessary than some other buildings for which provision is being made. I wish the Prime Minister would be good enough to tell us when he will be able to do something towards providing a suitable building.	x

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend has just said, our collection of national war memorial paintings is without doubt one of the finest that any country possesses, and certainly, I assume, the best collection anywhere of paintings in relation to the recent war. After my hon. friend brought the matter up last session the government did carefully look into the question of the housing of the paintings. We found, as has been represented by my hon. friend, that they were stored, in considerable part, in what is now the basement of the National Museum and Art Gallery. We also discovered that it was not a suitable place for storage, and that it was necessary, if the paintings were to be properly preserved, that they should be stored in a dry atmosphere and in a better environment generally. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Elliott) and his officers went carefully into the available accommodation in the city and were fortunate in being able to obtain some space in a part of the large Auditorium building. This part the government has leased for storing the paintings. The building is suited admirably for the purpose. It is fireproof, it has a southern exposure, is quite dry, and an even temperature can be readily maintained. From what the director of the art gallery says, I believe it will serve to keep the pictures in perfect condition. So much for the storage.	_ _
As for the exhibition of the paintings, that is another matter. Up to the present time the government has not felt it would be justified in asking parliament to appropriate money for an art gallery. There are many public buildings urgently needed. One of them was referred to by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) only a day or two ago-a building for the Supreme Court of Canada. There are other buildings necessary for departmental purposes, and we feel
we should consider meeting these requirements before undertaking a building for the exhibition of paintings. However, personally, I am not without hope that some public-spirited citizen will be found who one of these days will present the country with a national art gallery.

Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, in this morning's
Citizen the Prime Minister is reported as saying that Canada will not sign the optional clause until the mother country and the other dominions are ready to do so. I should like to know if he is correctly reported?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: OPTIONAL CLAUSE-PERMANENT COURT OF INTERNATIONAL JUSTICE
speechtext: I saw the report, Mr. Speaker, to which my hon. friend has just referred. I am afraid I have to say it is inaccurate. I remember being asked yesterday if I had anything further to add to the statement I made in the house a day or two ago as to Canada's position with respect to the optional cause, and I replied that the statement I had made in the house was all I had to say on the matter. The statement, I think, will bear out that all I said was that Canada was prepared to sign the optional clause, but did not intend doing so without conference with other parts of the British Empire, as had been promised at the time of the last Imperial conference; I made no statement to the effect that we would not sign the optional clause unless all parts of the empire agreed. Our view is that there should be a conference in the first place. After the conference it will be for us to say whether we shall sign alone, or whether it will be possible for all parts of the empire to sign at the same time.

If the board should report
to the minister that some of the manufacturers are not living up to the agreement will the minister promise us that he will take off the excise tax from all cars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend must not ask
me to commit myself in relation to what we may do in that regard in the next budget. Such a statement can be made properly only after approval on the part of the Governor General. However, my hon. friend may safely leave the matter in our hands. We have a pretty clear mind as to what should be done and it is just possible that the question may be considered in relation to the tariff inquiry now going on in connection, with steel and materials required in the manufacture of cars.

I wish we could feel better
satisfied to leave the matter in the minister's bands. We have done so for the last three years and some of us feel that for two years at any rate 'the manufacturers have been taking advantage of the elimination of the tax. The minister has been asleep at the switch and has allowed them to get away with it, to use a common expression. I do not think, therefore, that we should leave it to the minister until next session. Personally I should like to see the matter dealt with before this session is over. I wonder whether the minister would make the reference to the board wide enough so that they may report to him next year as to whether the customs tariff should not be further reduced on all motor trucks, which are coming into such general use to-day. As a matter of fact, to many farmers at any rate, the motor truck to-day takes the place which the wagon held some years ago. I would ask the minister to instruct the board to take up that question at the same time; the two matters could be considered together.

When this resolution
was last before the committee I asked the minister for a statement as to how the Canadian content was estimated. Supposing in the cheaper cars the Canadian content comprised 70 or 80 per cent: would that excess be applied to the higher priced cars with a Canadian content of say, 40 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter that belongs to the Department of National Revenue, but I have given instructions to the tariff board to look carefully into it also.

What has been the
practice in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I say, that matter is administered by the Department of National Revenue; they check up on the percentage of Canadian material going into the manufacture of cars.
But that does not afford me any information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I have sent for my colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler).

I am not
disposed to leave the minister in the position of evasion in which he has placed' himself. Consciously or unconsciously he has been guilty of a breach of faith with the members in this corner of .the house. When he appealed to us, in that memorable year, to permit him to relieve the automobile manufacturers in Canada to the extent of the removal of the excise duty he promised us absolutely, definitely and unquestionably that he would undertake to see that the manufacturers lived up to their agreement, which was to pass back to the consumers the saving which would result from the exclusion of the excise tax. The minister has now clearly shown in his answers to questions asked him that he has not checked up the manufacturers, but has relied .on casual letters which he has received from them, and that even at this moment he is not in a position to state whether in his opinion they have or have not lived up to their promise. Let me repeat the promise made 'by the Minister of Finance in 1926. He said:
We have, however, the right to reduce taxation, and if they do not live up fairly to this agreement we have the right to reduce the excise tax to all the trade of the world.
The hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) then asked:
Will that be inserted in the bill?
Mr. Robb:	It is not necessary.
It was not necessary, according to the minister, to insert it in the bill. The minister left the impression that he was prepared to remove the excise duty on imported cars if the manufacturers in Canada did not live up to their promise, and in the three years that have elapsed he has made no investigation whatever; he has undertaken no check whatever of the situation. He has relied solely upon opinions expressed in letters, and

No, but

have done and as it was his duty to do. During that session the situation as far as the administration was concerned was particularly strained, and to relieve the administration from a mighty ticklish position, to help the Minister of Finance, who is now pleased to smile about it, in one of the most critical moments in his career, and to meet his earnest request hon. members in this corner consented to modify their principles in this matter. Does the hon. gentleman
suggest that there was a barter between hon. members in that corner and the Minister of Finance?
Mr, IRVINE: I hope the hon. member for Bow River and all hon. members in this comer of the house will leam a much needed lesson in political economy and in .political matters generally from the question now before the house. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wonder if the minister realizes that a moment ago he said that this was a matter for the Minister of National Revenue, in spite of the fact that it was the Minister of Finance who sent a letter to the tariff board requesting them ,to deal with this matter, although it has to do with the collection of revenue. Why is it that our questions must go unanswered because the Minister of National Revenue is not here, while at the same time the Minister of Finance says, "Look what I have done; I have written to the chairman of the tariff board, who is a prospective Liberal candidate in a constituency which contains the largest automobile manufacturing industry in Canada, asking him to ascertain some of these .things for us." That is what the minister wants this house to believe, and this gentleman to whom the letter was written is the gentleman who, in his annual report as chairman of that board, states that he has established intimate relations with the manufacturers of this country. I may tell the minister that I propose to ask, before he gets through his resolutions, the names of the establishments

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
visited by that gentleman during the last twelve months, as mentioned in his report. We are going to ask for that information because we have a right to obtain it, and then we may find out exactly what are these intimate relations which have been established in this particular constituency 'between the largest manufacturers of automobiles in Canada and the chairman of the tariff board, a prospective Liberal candidate.
Does the minister think for a moment that the people of Canada will tolerate that sort of thing? Does he think that they will be deceived by it and that they will be made sport of in this way? A perfectly legitimate and proper question was asked in an endeavour to secure certain information, but the only reply we received was that the minister was referring the question to "dear Mr. Moore." The minister said to him, "You seek to represent a constituency in which is situated the largest automobile manufacturing business in Canada. Please go out and see how their prices compare with the prices paid in the United States, and! if you cannot do that, take a look at their books. Here is your authority to do so," but a moment ago it was the Minister of National Revenue who had to deal with this matter, rather than the Minister of Finance. To use the classical language which was indulged in by one of the members of the government the other day, you cannot play both ends against the middle in that way very long, so let us get down to brass tacks in connection with this matter. Did the minister say to Mr. Moore that last year Canada imported about $102,000,000 worth of automobiles and automobile parts? Did he observe that of that amount $55,000,000 represented automobile parts and the balance automobiles imported largely from the United States? Did he observe that our exports were sent to countries enjoying a preference under different treaties? Surely the minister must have observed these things; the questions asked are quite reasonable and I desire to associate myself with those who desire to have these questions answered. I do not like this bunkum of saying, "I passed it on to Mr. Moore," who wants to represent the constituency containing the largest automobile industry in Canada. It may get him some votes if he makes the right kind of a report.
Not many.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We will leave it at that.
Louder.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The minister and I were simply carrying on a little private conversation across the floor; he said I was getting information from another quarter, and I said I did not think so. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will that 'be a private
or public hearing?

Three years after a definite pledge is given to the house by the minister he says, "I will take the matter up with the tariff board and have an investigation made." It was the duty of the minister to have one of his own investigators make an investigation and not wait for the tariff board to inquire into this matter. The minister has the power to put a qualified man on the job to-day if he wants to do it. It is his duty to do that and not wait for the tariff board. It was his duty to have done that two years ago; it was his duty to have seen that this saving was passed on to the consumers as he promised it would be passed on, and the only way he could be sure thait that was done was by having a man from his department on the job from the day the

promise was made. In failing to do that he has broken faith with us and with the country. He has failed in his duty when he is unable to answer- the very simple question: Have they passed the saving back to the consumer? He was not able to answer that question and cannot answer it because he has no authoritative information. It was his duty as Minister of Finance, as an hon. member of the government and as one of the responsible ministers of the crown not only to keep the promise he made but to secure accurate information that the promise has been kept.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member forgets that it has not been established that they did not carry out their agreement. It is true that certain price lists were quoted from magazines showing a difference in price in Canada and in the United States. The hon. member will recall that when this was up last year I stated that I bad written to all the automobile manufacturers reminding them of the promise. Replies came in from most of them claiming that they were passing along this excise tax to their customers. I think there were two companies from which I did not receive replies. It happened that an official of one of those companies was either the president or secretary of the Automotive Association, and when I directed his attention to this fact he brought down my original letter acknowledging his reply. He had replied but the letter had been mislaid in the department, and it has not been found yet. He brought down a copy of the letter which he had sent and in that letter made the statement that he was passing this saving on.
And he also stated that the books were open to inspection at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. The Ford Motor Company had not replied at that time but their business was very much disturbed, as everyone knows. They have since claimed that eighty per cent, or nearly eighty per cent of the contents of their car is Canadian and they also claimed that they are passing the saving on. There are the statements which they make to be put up against the statements which have been made that they are not passing it on. In justice to the public I have instructed the tariff board to go into this matter carefully, to put auditors into the companies where they consider it necessary, and I told the chairman only the other day that in the public interest it would be better to have a public hearing. I am not disposed to condemn these men before they have been properly heard.

I have no fault to find with the minister for asking the advisory tariff board to examine very thoroughly into this matter. My criticism is that when this matter was brought to his attention he satisfied himself by writing letters to these automobile manufacturers. On April 12, 1928, the minister was asked by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner):
Is that all the minister has done?
Mr. Robb:	That is all.
Mr. Gardiner:	That is nothing.
It seems to me that nothing has been done in this case. I am very glad to hear the minister state that this matter will be made the subject of a public hearing and I presume the evidence will come before the members of the house. I am forced to express my regret that the minister has not seen fit to state to the house that if the case is proven that some of the automobile manufacturers have been taking advantage of this tax and have not passed the reduction on to the consumer, the government would remove the excise tax from all cars. I do not see in what other light the statements m'ade to the house in 1926 can be viewed. In answer to a question by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) the minister said:
We have, however, the right to reduce taxation, and if they do not live up fairly to this agreement we have the right to reduce the excise tax to all the trade of the world.
Mr. Evans:	Will that be inserted in the
bill?
Mr. Robb:	It is not necessary.
I do not know what other interpretation can be put upon the words of the minister. If he can give the house any other explanation of the remarks he made at that time I am sure we will be pleased to hear it.
If the minister will not remove by order in council the tax upon these cars which are being imported, when the case should be proved, I can only suppose that next year he intends to introduce another of those popular Robb budgets and is saving this change to make his budget popular. The budget which was described in the election campaign of 1926 as the popular Robb budget contained a reduction in the tariff on automobiles, and I am quite Satisfied that that was preeminently the one change which made that budget so popular. If that is the case, so far as the popularity of that budget is concerned, the success should not be ascribed to the Minister of Finance, it should be credited to -the members in this corner of the house who persisted' in keeping that matter before parliament and' finally persuaded the minister, perhaps against his own inclinations, to reduce the tariff on cars.

I would like to draw the attention of the minister to this further fact; they are charging the consumers of automobiles in the maritime provinces-I am satisfied they are doing the same thing in other parts of Canada-with a freight rate which is more than twice what the Ford Company or their agents pay on these cars, and in addition they include a delivery charge of $10. I have in my hand a couple of invoices for Ford cars which were sent to an agent at Glace Bay. The agent informed me that in every case the freight was less than $40 per car and yet the consumers in the maritime provinces are being charged $84 for freight and in addition to that they are being charged $10 for delivery charges. It may be argued that they are not contravening any statute of Canada when they do that, but if they are penalizing the consumer in the distant portions of Canada, for instance in the maritimes and the western provinces, with a freight charge which is more than twice what they are actually paying, it is time we carefully considered the question whether we should further protect this company from competition from other countries or not. To say the least, the practice is a most questionable one. When this question was debated on the floor of the house on April 12, one hon. member at least, seemed quite concerned for fear
the minister might remove this excise tax from imported cars, and subject Canadian manufacturers to a little more competition. He mentioned the fact that the Ford Company sustained a loss last year. In a letter which I have under my hand from an agent of the Ford Company, he says:
The company, as would be expected, did not pay a dividend last year, but, a few years back they were generous in the extreme. In addition to a 100 per cent cash dividend in 1911, they also paid 500 per cent in stock and followed this with a 600 per cent stock dividend in 1916. In 1924, when net earnings amounted to $53.13 a share, they paid 10 per cent, 20 per cent in 1925, 10 per cent in 1926, 15 per cent in 1927 and nothing in 1928 as would be expected.
He makes that statement because he knew they were reorganizing their factory at that time. He goes on:
However, if you will refer to ad., of the Canadian General Securities Corporation, appearing in all the daily papers in Canada on April 1 or 2, you will note that_ Mr. W. R. Campbell, president and treasurer, is quoted as stating that for January and February of this year, operations, "show net profits, after depreciation, in excess of $1,500,000-net profits for the month of March will be equally satisfactory-further it is estimated that the net profits after depreciation for the year 1929 will be in excess of any previous year."
That is the quotation which he gives. He suggests that it will be $10,000,000 at least. I do not think there is any occasion for the house or the minister to worry about 'the financial position of these companies. As a matter of fact, I think it is really important that 'the Minister of Finance should take some means of assuring the house that he will make good the promise which he made in 1926. I do not want to be unreasonable at all. If the minister thinks the case is not proven, I am quite willing that the matter should be investigated by the advisory tariff board. If we are to have an advisory tariff board in this country, perhaps it is the proper body to investigate this question. But I hope the minister will make a positive statement as to what he will do if the case is proven that these manufacturers have taken advantage of the remission of the excise tax and that he will assure the house that the tariff advisory board will be instructed to have brought out fully just what is the practice of these automobile corporations in setting the price which they charge to consumers in distant parts of Canada as related to their advertised list price at the factory, the price on which the excise tax and sales tax which they pay is based.

-but I should like my hon. friends to my left to explain to me how they know whether the manufacturers passed the excise reduction on to the consumer or not. I am going to submit a few outstanding facts in regard to the automobile business. My claim is that the government made a blunder as regards Canada when they undertook to tamper with the tariff on automobiles in 1926. This was detrimental to the industry as a whole and to the consumers of Canada as well.
No, no.

All right. Take the price of any automobile in 1926 when the government undertook to do something in regard to the tariff on automobiles; then go back three years and take the price of a similar automobile during that period and observe the drift of things. See what was going on in [Mr. Kaiser. 1
this country. Canadian manufacturers were grappling with a great industry and in those three years they reduced the prices of automobiles to Canadian consumers by nearly 40 per cent. How? By virtue of their own genius, by virtue of mass production and by virtue of internal economic administration they were endeavouring to give Canada a cheap automobile and they reduced the price by from 33^ to 40 per cent in those three years. If the automobile business had been left alone, what would have happened? Economics were being studied; genius was being developed; mass production was increasing, and the manufacturers were endeavouring to run their factories as many months in the year as possible. Immediately after this change the number of months of operation in the automobile business yearly was reduced and in our city for three or four months at a time when men were absolutely out of employment; whereas, if they had been at work all the year round they could, by thus reducing the yearly overhead costs, have produced automobiles at a more rapid pace and at a more reasonable price. In 1926, the government of Canada disturbed this wonderful industry. It listened to the croakers who were saying: Give us automobiles as cheap as they have them in the United States; reduce the price to the consumer. And my hon. friends think they have accomplished something. What have they done? The same type of automobile, the price of which was reduced between 30 and 40 per cent in those three years previous to 1926 has been manufactured and sold by the same people in Canada and the reduction in price has been less than 9 per cent in the last three years. If the government had left this industry alone, I have not the slightest doubt that the reduction in price would have been 20 or 25 per cent instead of 9. Because of the number of months in the year these people would have been employed, and because of the increase in mass production, the manufacturers could have reduced the price of their automobiles more rapidly than they have been able to do under present circumstances.
I see smiles on the faces of some hon. gentlemen. Evidently they think I am saying something that is absurd. I say to you gentlemen who are smiling that you desire to drive these industries out of Canada, but you will have another thought coming, and probably you will gat it inside of a week's time. The consumers of farm products in this country mean more to the farmers of Canada than do the consumers of any other country in the world. What has happened, for instance, in

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
the matter of automobile importations? Do hon. gentlemen smile ajt the fact that since the Minister of Finance made the change affecting automobiles in 1926 there has been an increase in the importation of the finished article amounting to over 260 per cent? Automobiles have been coming into this country in ever-increasing numbers, while the manufacturers in our own land could have manufactured right here at home every automobile that is used in Canada to-day, and in addition, they could have reduced the price by 20 per cent if they had been given a fair chance and were not continually assailed by people who think that our automobile manufacturers and manufacturers of every other article used ini Canada should be exposed to the competition of the whole world. I believe that we can make in Canada, and that we should make in Canada, everything that the people of Canada need, and if our industrial centres were left alone we would produce most of these goods just as cheaply as they are produced in the United States or anywhere else, but we cannot do it if our manufacturers are to be eternally disturbed by these absurd theorists. Our manufacturers cannot go on and develop industries in Canada if they are always to be assailed by people who believe that these goods should not be made in this country, but in some foreign land. Why should there have been this increase of 260 per cent in the importation of automobiles when our own manufacturers could make every automobile that is used in Canada. If this 260 per cent increase in automobile importations were not coming into this country, our factories would be able to run for one month longer in the year than they do at present. The theory that these articles should be manufactured in foreign countries instead of at home will not hold up against the facts; it will not even hold up against the consumers' idea of cheapness, because if we had been manufacturing all these automobiles in Canada we could have produced them almost as cheaply as in the United States or anywhere else in the world. How can we ever develop into a great country wthen such absurd trade theories are put into effect as those expounded by certain hon. gentlemen in this house?

I shall not attempt to deal
with the rash statements which have just been made by the hon. member for Ontario, but he did ask for information. He asked what led us to believe that the manufacturers of automobiles were taking advantage of the excise tax.
How do you know that the manufacturers are not passing this 5 per cent on to the consumer?
If the hon. member wouk only keep his seat warm, I would try anc tell him.
How do you know they do not pass it on?

I just got up to tell my hon. friend how I knew. If he would take the trouble to read the statement I placed on Hansard on April 12 last, he would see that the retail factory price of a Ford car in Canada is 29.1 per cent higher in the case of a coupe, 29.3 per cent higher in the case of a tudor sedan, and 29.8 per cent higher in the case of a fordor sedan.
Higher than what?
Higher than the price of the same car in the United States.
There is no comparison between the two cars. The Canadian car is a much better car than the United States car.

The customs tariff which
these men enjoy is 20 per cent. Now if the tariff is 20 per cent and the price in Canada is 29.1 per cent higher than in the United States, it seems to me that we have furnished enough proof to the Minister of Finance for at least an investigation to be made to determine whether or not these manufacturers have taken advantage of the excise tax.
There is no possible way of comparing the American Ford car with the Canadian, because the Canadian Ford car is so much better than the other.
In what w'ay?
It is better built and better in every way.

The tariff board could make a very thorough inquiry into this question. They could get the advice of mechanical engineers and ascertain just how much more expensive the Canadian Ford is than the American. May I point out to the hon. member from Oshawa (Mr. Kaiser) that in my statement in regard to this matter a year ago I said that apparently General Motors had lived up to this agreement. I had no proof to the contrary, and so I exempted them. I would say to the Finance minister that I cannot see why he is so anxious to continue to protect the automobile manufacturers, particularly at what might seem to be his own expense, because in every case when election time comes around these manufacturers cer-

tainly do not vote for the party of which my hon. friend is so prominent a member. I am perfectly unable to understand the attitude of the hon. member for Ohtario. I think he should thank the Minister of Finance for his attitude if he is really sincere.

I feel that this matter should not rest where it is. When this bargain was made, a definite and absolute promise was given to us here that the Minister of Finance at any time could exact the duty on these cars if he found that the reduction was not being passed on to the consumer. I feel that this action on the part of the automobile manufacturers is connived at by the government, and it is absolutely dishonest in the face of the whole country. The government is to-day conniving at the way in which these companies are putting if over the consumer. There is absolutely no necessity for any duty at all on cars entering Canada, because our Canadian manufacturers can compete with any part of the world. I listened a few days ago to a man from India who told us that the Canadian car was veiy much favoured there because of its cheapness, and it was. generally underselling the American car. Why is this? Is the Canadian consumer paying the Canadian manufacturer a duty so that he can dump his cars in other parts of the world? Is all the export trade of Canada to be everlastingly carried on at the expense of the Canadian consumer? Manufacturing to-day is being done cheaper in Canada in many cases than in the United States. I know of agricultural implements that are made in the city of Hamilton and sold in North Dakota, and our farmers can go across the boundary from Saskatchewan and buy a Hamilton drill in North Dakota, bring it back across the line, pay the duty, and save $30 by so doing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No.

I know that my hon. friend disputed this statement last year, but he has only to write to the research department of the United Farmers of Canada to get the facts. I say again that it is the Canadian consumer who is paying; he has to stand the burden of the whole export business of Canada. Our Finance minister put this over us three years ago when we from this corner demanded that the benefit of that excise tax be passed on to the consumer.
Now, why is it that this has got to be left so indefinite again for another two or three years, when there is absolutely no excuse at all for imposing a duty on the Canadian consumer ? Have the politics of our country come down to this state, that anything can be done that they can get away with? Is there no moral side to these questions at all? In my city, if there is one crime to-day more prevalent than another it is that young people are stealing cars for the sake of getting joy rides around the country. Afterwards they abandon the cars in a damaged condition. These young people show a spirit of utter irresponsibility. I want to ask the house today, where does that irresponsibility start? It starts right here on the treasury benches of this house; that is where it begins. It i3 not easy to say these things, but when a trick like that is put over us here, I cannot help saying that such a state of affairs should come to an end, and we should have something definite, particularly with regard to this matter. I do not intend to let these things go along as they have in the past.

Mr. Chairman, it was
not my intention to say anything in this debate, but I think statements such as the hon. member has just made should not be uttered in this house unless some proof is offered in support. Such statements do this country a lot of harm. Statements such as the hon. member made in a letter to the Montreal Gazette a week or two ago were a reflection on this whole house. Now I for one, want to protest against these allegations. Too often statements are made in this house that are absolutely ridiculous, and not a word of proof is given for them. The statements which the hon. member has just made are not new. I hold no brief for any manufacturer or any other person, but similar statements have been made from time to time for the last twenty years. What proofs have ever beep submitted in support? The only proof that I know of was supplied to this house, and it is on Hansard to-day. It was supplied by a former Finance minister, Sir Thomas White, who in answer to charges of this kind sent an officer of his department twice across this continent, once through the United States and then back through Canada, to get the market prices of agricultural im-

plements at different points in the two countries. He did so, and after making due allowance for difference in freight charges-
I am speaking from memory, it was a good many years ago-it was found there was very little difference between the prices in the United States and in Canada. Those figures are a matter of record of this house. And they are authoritative, because they were made by a responsible officer of the government. That report) is no doubt in the Finance department. In addition to that, we have statements by the manufacturers themselves, for instance, by the late general manager of the Massey-Harris company, absolutely contradicting the allegation and stating that never had they on any occasion sold their goods cheaper outside this country than inside. In face of that declaration we have men like the member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) getting up and making absurd, wild statements that, I submit, should not be made in any legislature in the world without proof. I say it is time that all this reckless talk upon any subject was stopped unless proof be submitted in support.
Hear, hear. I think the hon. member might take a little of that to himself.

I suppose we have the
last word now from the hon. member. But let me say that I can substantiate every statement I ever made in this house, which is more than members sitting opposite my hon. friend can do. I hold no brief for the manufacturers or for any other class in this country, but I do have some respect for the honesty of our manufacturers and of our people generally. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, this wild talk should cease unless some proof is forthcoming.

I write to confirm a cablegram which I sent to you on the 3rd inst. and in the following terms:-*
"Reference recent alteration tariff basis to 50 per cent; very anxious know if list raw material exceptions is being issued; please cable reply."

This federation has no doubt that this question's one which must have received or is now receiving your careful consideration, and as stated it will very much appreciate such information as you may be good enough to pass to it on this matter.

Head.
Overseas Organization.

London, January 2, 1929.
The Hon. J. A. Robb,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Robb,-
I think I can do no better than attach to this letter as I do copy of one which I addressed on the 6th December to the Minister of Customs. I have just received a reply from the Commissioner of Customs, in which he states that he is not in a position to add anything to the reply sent to the cablegram referred to in the attached letter, except to suggest that it might be as well to communicate direct with yourself on the matter, as it is one which falls within your purview.
My letter to the Minister of Customs covers a question which, important as it was early in December, is becoming increasingly so now.
I shall be grateful of on behalf of this federation you would advise me whether you have any such list in contemplation as that referred to in my letter to the Minister of Customs. In addition to the manufacturers referred to in that letter as using raw material totally unprocurable in this country, there are also some manufacturers who use as material raav to themselves products upon which a certain amount of initial w-ork has been expended at the source overseas from which such materials are procured. Users of certain materials of this nature are becoming nervous, because they fear that they may not be able to certify that of the completed article exported to Canada, more than 50 per cent can be attributed directly to British material and British labour.
Very similar questions have arisen in the past with the dominions of New Zealand and Australia, both of which, as you are aware, give, as does Canada, a preference to goods of British manufacture. Various discussions have taken place over a period of time. As the result of these in the cases of both of those dominions, lists such as I refer to have been issued by them. I mentioned this fact because if, as we trust, this question of the issue of a list by yourselves in receiving or will receive favourable consideration by you, the results of those discussions to which I refer are available either through the board of trade here in London or otherwise.
The question is regarded as one of very great importance amongst manufacturing interests in this country, w'hich is my reason for troubling you at such length.
The federation will look forward with the greatest interest to the reply you may be good enough to send to this letter.
(Signed) J. Moir Mackenzie.
I will read a cablegram from the same gentleman, dated January 18, 1929, to the Hon. James Robb, Minister of Finance, Ottawa, as follows:

Is there any reply to that?

There is the usual reply that one might expect. There is another letter from the same gentleman addressed from London under date of February 25, 1929, to the Hon. J. A. Robb, Minister of Finance, Ottawa. In part, this letter reads:
In common with all other trade associations, members of this federation, the Association of British Chemical Manufacturers, 166 Piccadilly, London, W.L, was informed of the recent alteration in basis in the British preferential tariff.
Then the writer refers to an interview he had with a representative of chemical manufacturers, and he says:
I explained to my caller that as far as we were aware, the government of Canada w'as not prepared to issue a list of this description. He then raised specifically the question of mercury and its compounds. He pointed out that mercury is unprocurable from empire sources and that as a constituent it enters into innumerable compounds of a chemical nature, being either the predominant factor as regards value or at any rate being a very considerable factor.
I informed my caller that as far as information available in this country at the present time went, I thought that what was in the minds of the authorities in Ottawa was that each such compound wrould have to be considered on its own merits and a decision given covering such a compound.
A further conversation took place betw-een Mr. Pratt and myself, when he pointed out that the number of such compounds containing mercury was a very large one indeed and was being continually added to as new specifics are produced.
I asked him if he would write to me on the matter, and this he has now done. On behalf,

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
therefore, of the Association of British Chemical Manufacturers, I would ask you to be kind enough to give consideration to the case as put by him in his own words, as follows: -
_ "I should like to have a ruling on the following point of principle in connection with the submission of special cases on behalf of this association.
If we take the case of mercury compounds as an example, we find that the raw material, namely mercury, is not obtainable commercially within the empire. In most mercury compounds, the cost of the metal itself will constitute more than 50 per cent of the cost of the final product."
There is a tong brief dealing with the matter. I wilt now read a memorandum handed to the minister by the British High Commissioner in this city. This is dated from the High Commissioner's office, Ottawa, January 28, 1929, and it reads:
After a careful examination of the new Canadian regulations governing the grant of imperial preference to goods entering Canada from Great Britain. His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom are of the opinion that the application of these regulations on first February would result in an unfortunate dislocation of trade.
Conscious of the motives of the Canadian government in framing and announcing the new regulations for the benefit of inter-imperial trade His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom desire to suggest that the regulations m question should not be brought into operation until first April or first May-, thereby enabling traders to adjust themselves to the new conditions and at the same time to fulfil forward contracts the raw material for which will have been ordered some time before the new regulations were announced.
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom have further ascertained that the following goods, amongst others, which are manufactured wholly m the United Kingdom, will be unable to qualify for imperial preference because the raw materials, which are unobtainable in the United Kingdom in commercial quantities, exceed 50 per. cent of the total value of the manufactured article:-
Manufactures of copper and its alloys, cotton yarns up to 40 counts, grey cotton piece goods, certain types of silk goods, paper manufactures and electric cables. Detailed particulars to support the statement that the goods for which exemption is asked are wholly manufactured in the United Kingdom and that the raw materials are not obtainable in the United Kingdom in commercial quantities are being prepared in London for the information of His Majesty's government in Canada; but pending their receipt the High Commissioner in Canada for His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom nas been instructed to put forward very earnest request for exemption of the goods mentioned above from the new Canadian regulations, or the modification of the latter in such a manner as will enable goods wholly manufactured in the United Kingdom from the above raw materials to continue to benefit by- Canada's traditional policy of preference for British empire manufactures.

There are further complaints in the correspondence, and it is not surprising that no recent complaints have been made, because the minister has not dealt with those that have already been forwarded-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What justification has my hon. friend for saying that the minister has not dealt with the complaints?
There is nothing on the file to show, and the minister has not said that he has dealt with them. Will he tell us now whether the matter has been dealt with and whether such a list has been published?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I informed the house a few moments ago that the Department of National Revenue had a man in England who was looking into all these cases as they came before us, but since then we have had no complaints from the overseas boards. I understand that the officer is now on the way home. I imagine when he returns, we shall have the report, but I repeat that while my hon. friend has read from a long list of statements which have come from overseas, he has not made out any case that British importations have been stopped. My hon. friend has read some statements wherein it is claimed that certain goods were not obtainable in the United Kingdom. The British High Commissioner made the same statement to us, but we told him frankly that the United Kingdom did not comprise the whole British Empire, and that certain goods, if they were not obtainable in the United Kingdom, as we knew they were not, were obtainable in Canada and in South Africa. I will admit at once, as I admitted before, that there may be cases where we will have to make modifications, but we are not going any further than some of the other British dominions. Australia requires 75 per cent, New Zealand 50 per cent and the mother country herself requires 75 per cent on certain optical goods going in there from here. I am not sure just what South Africa requires. Surely it is not unreasonable on behalf of the British workingman to see to it that so far as possible British workingmen are employed within the United Kingdom if the reduced tariff is to be taken advantage of. When I brought this measure in before, I told my hon. friend that our attention had been directed to the fact that the British preference was getting into disrepute even among the British workingmen. Why? Because the goods were brought in from non-preference countries, indeed from

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
countries with which Canada had not a favoured trade agreement. They would do a little work on them, repack the goods on the wharves, perhaps at Liverpool or some other shipping point, and then ship them to Canada as British goods. I am sure that my hon. friend desires, as we all do, that if we are to give a British preference it should be as far as possible a preference for British goods, and it is not unreasonable to ask that there be 50 per cent of British labour and material, the labour in the United Kingdom and the material from anywhere within the empire. There may be cases where it is not obtainable, but these cases will be adjusted when the report of the officials of the department investigating the matter comes before us. That report has not yet been presented.

I have no complaint to make of the regulations in so far as they stimulate inter-imperial trade. Our complaint has been on the ground that this regulation impedes inter-imperial trade. The Minister of Finance refers to South Africa, New Zealand and some of the other dominions, but those dominions have exempted a list of goods which are not commercially procurable within the British Empire. That is the whole argument. Take velvet, for instance. In the raw it is procurable in Japan. It is brought to England and manufactured there, but the raw material is more than 50 per cent, and under this regulation it could not come in under the British preference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The British government has not brought that to my attention so far as my recollection goes.

No douibt there are a great many other commodities that have not been brought to the minister's attention. It seems to me that at the very time when the United States are proposing to increase their tariff against our natural products, it would be good business for us to make it as easy as possible for the British people to buy our products, instead of putting into effect a regulation that certainly will have the effect of impeding inter-imperial trade. Until such a list is published and until certain of these goods are exempted from its application, this regulation must certainly interfere with trade from the mother country, and will prevent many British goods from coming in and getting the advantage of the British preference.

Customs tariff-779a.	Copper rods when
imported by manufacturers for use in their own factories in the manufacture of electrical conductors, the individual units of such electrical conductors not to exceed the area of No. 7/0 gauge conductor, per pound: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, i cent; general tariff, J cent.

I made reference to this item when I was speaking on the budget and I endeavoured to explain the situation in regard to copper rods. I will go over this again in order to refresh the minds of the hon. members. Copper bars are the finished product of the smelter and the raw material of the rolling mill which rolls them into copper rods. Copper rods in their turn a.re the raw material of the copper manufacturers. The situation is something like this:	A small ring of men in the United
States control 95 per cent of the copper output of the world. They do not mine it but they control the output and they export copper bars to other countries at a higher price than they sell to their own people in the United States. The purpose in doing that is this: they want to fix the price of copper the world over. If they fixed it in the United States, they would run foul of their antitrust law. Therefore they fix the price for export, and then each one goes back to his own office and quotes for home consumption in the United States a price $8 a ton less than the price he quotes people in other countries.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Five dollars a ton.

Well, that makes my argument that much stronger. There is located in Brockville one concern which rolls copper bars into copper rods. It employs some thirty-one men in that work. It receives 60 per cent of its raw material from the smelter at Trail in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is it not fair to say
that they did, but they do not now? I think the record shows that.
Why not now?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Because they have discontinued manufacturing that raw material at Trail.

Does my hon.
friend mean to say that copper is no longer smelted at Trail?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is smelted, but not refined to the extent that would make it available as raw material for that particular plant. I think that was the evidence of the Mr. Phillips people.

That was not
the understanding I had of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am just asking the hon. gentleman if that is not the fact.

My understanding was that they get 60 per cent from Trail and that they have to purchase the other 40 per cent in the United States; that the smelter at Trail is not under the control of this copper ring, and therefore does not charge this excess price. But this concern in Canada has to pay an excess price of $5 a ton on its copper bars and then when it comes to sell its rods it is met by the competition of concerns in the United States who get their raw material at a lower price but who do not pay any duty on the rods coming into Canada. The proposal now is to charge on copper rods a duty of half a cent a pound, or $10 a ton. This is the raw material of no less than five factories which are using copper rods in Canada. The concern at Brockville employing thirty-one men is handicapped to the extent of $5 a ton and the proposal is to offset this handicap by putting double that rate, or an additional $10 a ton, on the raw material of five different factories in Canada. The concern in Brockville is handicapped on only 40 per cent of its raw material. These other concerns, if this duty is added, will be handicapped on 100 per cent of their raw material. This would be equal to multiplying the handicap by five and placing it on another branch of the same industry. I do not think this is economically sound, and I would suggest that the minister let the item stand over.

subsubtopic: RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
I argued the case of Cook versus Cook before the Privy Council. The courts of Alberta had decided that a wife might, under the Matrimonial Clauses Act, obtain a divorce for herself. The Privy Council, following the decision, the House of Lords in the Jeffrey case, reaffirmed the old doctrine that the domicile of, the wife was that of the husband and that there could be no domicile for her other than that of the husband, wherever that domicile might be. During the progress of the argument it was observed by one of the law lords that the only way in which the matter could be dealt with would be by the parliament of Canada. As the Minister of Justice has said, there is undoubtedly such a thing as two domiciles. There is the law of domicile with respect to the distribution of property, but we are not dealing with that here. I suppose there is no harm in saying that I discussed this matter with the hon. gentleman who introduced the bill, and also with the law officers. I think the most important words have been struck oqt, and they are, "for the purposes of this act a married woman. . ." This is an act which deals with the domicile in divorce matters, and this parliament would have jurisdiction. I quite agree with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and the hon. Minister of Justice that we would be exercising powers entirely beyond our jurisdiction, so far as the British North America Act is concerned, unless we say that we are only legislating for the purposes of this act, that is, for divorce purposes.
The hon. Minister of Justice is opposed oh principle to divorce, and the other evening he placed his position before the house with

Divorce Proceedings-Domicile
respect to the general principles regarding domicile in a manner to which no exception could be taken. He stated what the highest court of the realm has pronounced to be the law, having regard to t'he provisions of the statute under which we in Alberta exercise jurisdiction in divorce matters, namely, the English Divorce Act of 1857. Under the act of 1857 it was declared that a woman who was separated from her husband-1 did not intend to participate in this debate and I have not the time to send out for the section- should have all the rights of a femme sole and she could contract or do as she pleased. Since that time the position of married women has greatly changed. Under the provisions of the law in the provinces of Alberta, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Ontario, and the maritime provinces-I cannot speak with authority with respect to Quebec-a woman has a separate existence under the Married Women's Property Act with respect to property, with respect to contract and with respect to all rights which make her, in the eyes of the law, an individual apart from her husband. Up to the present time the law of the Dominion as to domicile has been that the domicile of the wife is that of the husband, and in the divorces granted by this parliament the question of domicile has been established on the basis of the domicile of the husband. This parliament has declined to grant divorces in more cases than one because the husband was domiciled in the United States of America, and that, under British law, being the domicile of the wife it followed that the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada had disappeared. This bill merely proposes to carry into divorce legislation the principle of which has been adopted in each province of confederation, namely, to confer upon the wife, when she has been abandoned and is living separate and apart from her husband as a femme sole, the right to acquire for herself a domicile.
Leaving that question for the moment, what is a domicile? I think many members of the house look upon, residence and domicile as being one and the same thing. There are two factors which determine domicile; one is actual residence in a .particular place and the other is the intention. Although there may be a residence for fifty years, if the second factor, namely, intention, is absent there is no domicile established. The leading case in that connection is that of an American who went from Philadelphia to the United Kingdom and lived there for thirty or forty years. When he died it was contended that he was domiciled in England. It was successfully set up that
he had never lost his United States domicile, because during his lifetime he had declared that he intended to return to the United States, and always spoke of that and no other as his country. Although there had been a residence of, I think, something over thirty years in the United Kingdom, there was no presence of the second factor that makes domicile, namely, the intention to remain there as his home. That is, the intention is the all-important matter.
Here is a case of a wife who is abandoned; she is living separate and apart from her husband. She may be judicially separated or she may not. She is living alone. This bill declares-and the words "for the purposes of this act" are all-important; without them the bill is I think, ultra vires of this parliament- that for t'he purposes of this act, namely, for the purpose of divorce, first, the British principle remains; that is, if the point at which she was abandoned by her husband was his domicile, that is her domicile. If she was abandoned in Alberta, her domicile is Alberta; if she was abandoned in Saskatchewan, her domicile is Saskatchewan; if she was abandoned in Manitoba, her domicile is Manitoba. Then we say what the Supreme court of the United States said, I think in 1868; what state courts in the United States have held for many years; what the Dominion of New Zealand1 said some years ago, since overruled by the decision in Cook versus Cook, namely, that this woman may now exercise the rights of a femme sole. In other words, she may exercise the same rights as though she had never been married. She may acquire a domicile of her own. How? First, by remaining in a particular community as her home; and then, with the intention of remaining there indefinitely.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Under the present law the Manitoba courts have jurisdiction to pronounce divorce only when both parties are domiciled in Manitoba.

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has certainly indicated what the obvious result is; namely, that by this legislation the wife, being a femme sole, being abandoned by her husband, being no longer under his protection, her status being

still that of a married- *woman, as the minister has well said, may change that to the extent of acquiring a domicile as though she were a single woman. That is all. Then we say that, she having acquired that domicile, the courts of that country have at once jurisdiction, as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre says over her matrimonial state, that is, they have the right to divorce her from her husband. As I say, the supreme court of the United States, I said in 1868 but I think as a matter of fact it was 1870, declared that one of the incidents that resulted from the widening of 'the rights of married women was that, when abandoned, she could acquire a domicile of her own. Our courts have, as the minister 'has said, declared1 exactly the opposite, and this parliament has the power to deal with the matter. The question is, shall it exercise that jurisdiction? But it has not the right to exercise this power, as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George says, unless such power is limited to divorce that is for the purposes of the act and the act only. To that extent it is an addition to the existing legislation which is British legislation of 1857. Therefore I am perfectly certain, unless we do this, the very injury which the Minister of Justice desires to avoid will continue, namely, we shall have people leaving Canada, going to the United States, setting up a fictitious domicile and securing a divorce with all the consequences incident thereto and all the uncertainties as to the legitimacy of the offspring. That is a very serious matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext: I would rather have the United States assume the responsibility than ourselves.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: RIGHT OF MARRIED WOMEN TO ESTABLISH DOMICILE
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice and I differ in that regard, I would rather be a party to this legislation to give legality to the situation than become a party to the scandals that, we know, exist with reference to it. That is my reasoning in arriving at a conclusion in the matter. I admit the force of the hon. gentleman's reasoning and of the objection of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. On the other hand, I can give half a dozen cases that come to my mind. One is that of a woman living in Alberta who has been abandoned by her husband. She has no idea where he is. The courts hold that if he is a roving person and has no known domicile, the domicile of his origin is the domicile that attaches to him, because the law is that every man is born with a domicile and is never without it. So it was held in the Cook case that this roving husband who was at one time domiciled in 
Alberta, although he changed his mind and roved about, had the domicile of his origin, namely, Ontario, and therefore the Alberta court could not deal with the matter.
What we are doing is to decide whether or not we desire to have a condition continued with all the scandal that attaches to it, with men and women going to a foreign jurisdiction, setting up fictitious domiciles, obtaining divorces in those courts which divorces are valid in every part of the United States, by reason of its constitution, sometimes marrying in the United States and coming back to Canada, confronted with the uncertainty of their own position and that of their children. We have to choose between that and the enactment of a statute whereby we declare that a woman who, in her own province, is a separate person with respect to contracts, obligations, debts, sitting in parliament, holding any office which may be in the gift of the people-and under our statutes she is eligible for any office except that she may not as yet sit in the senate-shall be given this additional right, namely, that of acquiring for herself for the purposes of this act a domicile. So far as I am concerned, I am in favour of giving her that right to acquire a domicile in order that her status, which is that of a single person with respect to contracts, obligations, property and everything that concerns her existence as a citizen, may be the same for the purpose of a domicile for the purpose of securing a divorce. In that way let us prevent the scandals to which I have referred and say that a woman who is abandoned by her husband may acquire a domicile for the purposes of this act, namely, a divorce act, and for any purpose concerning property in any way, shape or form. I think proper words could be found to express that meaning and we could pass this bill at this session.
Progress reported.

I should like to ask the

There is a situation in connection with this matter that I would like to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee. I understand quite well that the only smelter in Canada that does produce copper bars is the Trail smelter of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. Their supply of copper has come until recently almost exclusively from the Granby Copper Company at Allen'by. Some two million dollars' worth of copper is produced there annually. I quite understand that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company could not supply the demand of Canadian manufacturers for copper bars at the present time for the very good reason that all the
copper now produced by the Granby Copper Company is exported from Canada in its raw state to the Tacoma smelter. I desire to bring this matter as forcibly to the attention of the government as I can, for I believe that when we have in Canada smelters capable of refining our raw mineral wealth, those smelters should be utilized.
I quite realize, too, that there may be a dispute between these two companies as to the terms and conditions upon which this ore should be smelted, but I realize also that it is quite possible for this government to bring these two concerns together and to tell the Granby company that the exportation of copper in its raw state will not be tolerated, and to tell the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company that it must accept the ore of the Granby company and refine it on a fair basis. A fair basis could easily be arrived at by arbitration between the two companies. This is a situation which in my opinion merits the consideration of this government. If, for instance, we were smelting our raw copper at home, there would be no necessity for going down on our hands and knees to the United States for these copper bars. There would be no necessity for us to say to the United States:	So long as you
sell your copper bars to us at a price higher than you sell them in your home market we will put our tariff against your copper rods. This is what we are telling them. This is retaliation. We are going down on our hands and knees to the United States, whereas the root of the trouble lies in the fact that we do not insist on the refining of our raw copper at home.
I would draw further to the attention of this government that British Columbia at the present time is the greatest producer of copper in Canada. That may not long be the case, because Saskatchewan and Manitoba, through the medium of such properties as the Hudson Bay and Sherritt-Gordon will become gTeat copper producers. Ontario, through the medium of International Nickel, will also become a great copper producer. Canada bids fair to become one of the greatest copper-producing countries in the world, and British Columbia should be an example to this government in that connection. We are producing there to-day twelve million dollars' worth of copper per annum. A large proportion of this copper is going out of British Columbia in its raw state, unsmelted. We have across the harbour from Vancouver the Britannia Mining Company, producing about five million dollars' worth of copper per annum, all of which is going out of this

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
country in its natural state. That is quite a sufficient quantity of copper to justify the erection of a smelter, and I suggest to this government that it is its duty to advise the Howe Sound company that that condition will not be tolerated beyond a certain period. I do not think we need put any export duty on this raw material. All we have to do is to tell them that we will not have our raw mineral wealth going out of this country unrefined. Give them ample time in which to finance a smelter and the thing will be done, and Canada generally will benefit by such a policy. The reason it is necessary for us today to introduce a resolution such as that before the committee is because we have failed to take advantage of our natural wealth and failed to make provision for the refining of that wealth even to some extent here in our own country. The time has come when the Canadian people demand that such steps be taken. They want their raw materials fabricated at home. That is a natural desire, and one which the government should take notice of.
Mr. McGIBB'ON:	As the Minister of
National Revenue is in his place I would like to ask him for some information which I have tried unsuccessfully to get from the Minister of Finance a number of times, namely, as to the basis of arriving at the Canadian content of cars made in Canada.

speechtext: I am not sure that I understand exactly what the hon. gentleman desires, ibut I take it that he refers to the excise tax of 5 per cent, which is remitted in certain cases on cars manufactured in Canada. Am I right in that?

I have given information as' to the first; that is, that the 5 per cent exemption is granted on cars selling for $1,200
or less.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend's question is as to how that Canadian content is arrived at, whether on the average of all the cars or on each individual car.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: A number of cars selling for less than $1,200 are manufactured in the same factory. We take the factory output of. all cars of $1,200 and under, and they must qualify as to 50 per cent Canadian content before the exemption is granted. With regard bo the fifty per cent content which is demanded before the drawback is payable on raw materials entering into those cars, it works out in practice the same way. The drawback is not granted until the fifty per cent is checked up.

The minister does not
understand me. For instance, take General Motors. The Chevrolet is one of their low priced cars, and more than fifty per cent of it is made in Canada; some of their other oars contain less than fifty per cent. Do you take the average over the shop or the individual car?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: We very seriously considered what the basis should1 'be. Obviously it is impossible to take the individual oar and follow it from the outset right through to completion. It is impossible to check all the materials that enter into each car. Then we were faced with the question whether we should take each particular line of car-my hon. friend mentioned General Motors-such as the Chevrolet, the O'ldsmobile, the Oakland, the Pontiac, and others separately or whether it might be advisable for a number of reasons to interpret the law in such a way that we would take the total factory output, and then make all the output qualify on the fifty per cent basis before the company could get the drawback on their imported raw materials. After careful consideration-and I may say after consultation with some of my hon. friends opposite-as to the best thing to do, we adopted the factory output method. There has been a little criticism from one quarter alone. There has been no discrimina-don. At any rate, we have followed that plan.
Does the minister think that is legal?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
I do not think there is any
doubt about the legality of it at all. I do not see wherein the difference lies just because a certain make of car is called by a

certain name. General Motors might call their cars all by the name McLaughlin-Buick Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, instead of, we will say, Chevrolet, Pontiac, Gldsmobile, Oakland, McLaughlin-Buick, and all the rest of them. However, there may be some difference of opinion, and as a matter of fact we are going to review the whole situation.
I might perhaps briefly state our reasons for taking the course I have mentioned. A good many of these cars, for example, the Chevrolet, and some other cars made by other concerns, contain away above fifty per cent Canadian content; some of them, on the other hand, would prohafely fall below the fifty per cent. We will take a oar, for example, like the LaSalle.
Mr. MicGIBBON:	Or the Cadillac.

Yes, or the Cadillac. If
you did not allow them to average the factory content over the whole seven lines made by General Motors, the result would be, as we considered it-I think quite correctly-that the higher priced cars would not be made in Canada at all; there would be no work done on them here; they would be imported in the finished condition, with the result that just that much labour would be lost to this country. There is the added result that to bring the total factory output up to fifty per cent, some of the lines being below that figure, on the other lines they would have to go still higher in order to obtain the average. That was one of our reasons for adopting the factory output method, to ensure that some work on the higher priced cars would be performed in Canada.
