I hope the minister will reconsider the whole tariff situation regarding copper. No doubt in the not far distant future conditions in Canada will be very different from what they are to-day. There will be smelting, and we shall have copper produced in Canada in the form of ingots, bars, and so on. But that is not the condition at the present moment. Therefore one is forced to consider and in the meantime to guard the interests of our brass founders. They are dependent upon the United States for their copper. Why? Because Canada does not produce nearly sufficient raw material- copper ingots-for the brass founders. Previous to the war the raw material, in the form of
, Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
ingots, was imported free of duty. During the war a duty was imposed which is now something like one and a half cents a pound. That duty has continued up to the present time. Consequently our brass founders to-day are paying one and a half cents per pound on their copper-one and a half cents per pound for their raw material. There has been no increase in duty on the finished product. Therefore the brass founders have had a difficult course to pursue. I wish the minister would specially think of this; is it well to have a duty of one and one half cents per pound on copper, which is the raw material for the bras3 founders, the workers in copper and brass? I think not. I think there is much in the argument that so long as Canada fails to produce a sufficient amount of raw material in the form of ingots, the government might well do without the duty on copper in that form. Then there is this other advantage. The item before us is copper rods. Were the duty taken off ingots, it would be a strong incentive to our people to do their own refining and to produce their own rods and bars. It is an additional reason,
I think, why at the present time we should remove the duty on copper ingots. Certainly it would be for the advantage of the brass founders, but also it would stimulate the production of refined copper. At the present time our copper and brass workers are in great doubt whether it is of advantage to them to manufacture their own products or pay a duty and import them.

The Minister of National
Revenue has told us very clearly how he arrived at the Canadian content of cars. I judge that he has such a staff that he is able to go into the cost of all cars and to ascertain what relation the cost of production bears to the price charged. If that is the case, I submit that in these matters we shall get much more satisfaction through this department than through the tariff board, in regard to whether or not the excise tax has been passed on to the public. The tariff board, I presume, would only avail themselves of the officials of the revenue department. Therefore I suggest to the government if they want to get at the bottom of whether this excise tax is being passed on to the public or retained by the companies they would be much better served by the revenue department. I should like to hear what the Minister of National Revenue has to say about it, but perhaps he is too modest to speak.

Let us get back once more
to copper rods and let us hear from the government what their policy is with respect

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
to the processing of copper in our country At one time the Consolidated Smelters at Trail obtained copper from the Granby Company, the purchases running into millions each year, but owing to a slight dispute between these two concerns that copper ore is now going to the United States and Canada is suffering in consequence. Surely that dispute could be adjusted. I know of no argument in answer to the case put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. Let these companies be told, "We will give you two years to erect your smelters and treat copper ores in Canada; if not we shall take some means to see that you are penalized for not doing so". There is no reason why this should not be done; it would mean employment for many more people in Canada and would be a businesslike proceeding. I would do the same thing with the asbestos deposits in Quebec.
Here we also have an unsatisfactory state of affairs. The United States government have announced their intention to levy a 25 per cent ad valorem duty on shingles entering the United States and this means that our cedar logs will go there and be manufactured into shingles. What will this government do about that? What will they do in regard to the pulpwood situation, which has been brought to their attention time and time again on the floor of this house by myself and others? Is it not time that we looked forward to doing something to retain our people in Canada instead of allowing them to go across the line? Let us build up industries in Canada so that the sons of our farmers will have something to turn to when they graduate from the farms instead of having to leave this country in order to make a livelihood south of the line. It is time we received an answer to this argument, and so far I have heard not one from hon. gentlemen on the government side. What is the opinion of the Minister of Finance with respect to these vital questions? I consider them among the vital questions that confront us to-day in this Dominion.

I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard and with the hon. member who has just spoken as to what would be the real and permanent remedy in a case of this kind, namely, an export duty on copper. That would obviate the necessity of an application to the government, of any order in council, or of anything such as is proposed in this resolution.

A duty on
copper ore?

state. Have it refined and finished in Canada. Let us refine our raw material so as to give employment to our own people; let us reduce it as far as possible in this country.

A matter of

Does my hon. friend propose to forbid them to sell cheaply and also to sell dearly?

I propose to forbid them to trim us both ways, first by dumping and then 'by charging an exorbitant price for what we cannot buy in Canada. My hon. friend
says in this matter we are trying to overrule the finding of the tariff board, and I want to draw his attention to the fact that this is a case where the tariff board justifies its existence. That board found the facts, which are contained in the evidence; we have read the evidence and it is our duty now, as responsible members of parliament, to decide what we will do in the face of that evidence. Hon. gentlemen opposite are fond of talking about building up Canadian industry, and this is how they propose to assist the Canadian mining industry: First they say to the prospector, "We will tax you on all the took and equipment you require before you can go out and look for mines.."

Talk about the issue.

I am coming to it. Then, when the mine is found, they say to the company, "We will tax you an excessive rate on all the equipment and machinery you require for your mine." Then, after the mine has been developed through the expenditure of millions of dollars and after devoting years of work to it, they say to the company, "We will forbid you to sell your ores except to Canadian smelters." Customs tariff-113. Cocoanut, desiccated, unsweetened, per pound: British preferential tariff, 2 cents; intermediate tariff, 3 cents; general tariff, 3 cents.
Will the minister mow tell us where the request for these changes came from?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose we will consider the two items 'together. Under the present tariff, desiccated cocoanut, sweetened or not, enters under item 113 at 5, 6 and 6 cents, chiefly from the island of Ceylon. Application was made for reduction on the unsweetened, it being represented at the public sittings that, in the case of the unsweetened, the specific duty at present operative had an ad valorem effect of about 60 per cent. It is proposed by means of the two items, 112 and 113, to reduce the duty on unsweetened or less highly processed cocoanut, without changing in any way the sweetened. Imports of desiccated cocoanut, sweetened or unsweetened, in 1928, were valued at $193,000, of which $180,000 came from Ceylon. Application was made to the tariff board by Dodwell and Company of Vancouver, supported by the Consumers League. There was no opposition.

When these items first
came up I made the statement to the Minister of Finance that these changes meant a clear gift to the Dodwell Company of $66,000 per annum. I asked the minister to let the item stand over for a while, and he kindly consented. I take issue with the minister on this item, on the ground! that this is a type of case which occurs so often in connection with the tariff, whereby we are led to believe that the tariff is being reduced when it is actually being raised to the ordinary consumer. In support of my statement I have before me the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Let me say, first of all, that the agent for the Consumers' League was unaware that an application had been made for a reduction simply on the raw product. The rates under item 113 as it stood before on cocoanut, whether sweetened or unsweetened, were 5, 6 and 6 cents. That is reduced to 2, 3 and 3 cents. We had no idea that that did not apply to the whole of item 113. But when the question comes before us in committee of the whole house we find that the two items have been split, and that the sweetened as before retains the higher tariff, and the unsweetened retains the low tariff, giving to the only manufacturer of this com-
modity that I know of in Canada this super bonus of S66,000. At page 7 of the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the year ending December 31, 1928, I find there were 2,210,041 pounds of cocoanut, desiccated, sweetened or not, imported into Canada at a value of $159,228. That works out to a price of 7J cents per pound. Now when the tariff is reduced to 2, 3 and 3 cents, the manufacturer is given a distinct advantage of 3 cents a pound, and as he is the only importer and the only manufacturer of this commodity in Canada, it means that he can take out of the pockets of the 'Canadian consumers a clear profit of $66,000. That figure is obtained by multiplying 2,210,041 pounds by 3 cents. That represents a clear gift of [DOT]$66,000 to the manufacturer for importing the cocoanut, sprinkling a little sugar on it, and then calling it a manufactured article. If you look a little further into the matter, and transform the specific duty into an ad valorem duty, you will find that it works out to an ad valorem duty of 82 per cent. There is no article that I know of in the tariff which merits a duty of 82 per cent. It is simply absurd in the extreme. It will be seen by this that the ultimate consumer is entirely left out of consideration. We hear a great deal about the low tariff policy of our friends of the Liberal party, but surely the consumer should be given some consideration in the matter. Both sweetened and unsweetened were equal before; they should be equal now. It is discrimination and it is ridiculous for a party that calls itself a low tariff party. This 82 per cent gives one company a monopoly of the business. I have brought this up because it clearly shows what is coming to one manufacturer and what is coming to the other. In respect to a great many of the articles where the tariff is reduced, it is reduced only on the article which the manufacturer himself uses, and the corresponding reduction of duty to the consumer is not granted; he does not reap that advantage because the manufactured article itself is not reduced by the same amount. Let me take an instance where one manufacturer gets-a 10 per cent reduction on his raw material. In such a case surely that reduction should be passed on the ultimate consumer. For example, if the tariff on the manufactured article was 35 per cent before the reduction, then the price to the ultimate consumer should be correspondingly reduced. I have taken this case because in every instance that I know of the manufacturer gets the advantage and the ultimate consumer does not. In this case the sole manufacturer

of the sweetened article, Dodwell and Company, is getting $66,000 out of the pockets of the ultimate consumers of Canada. I would ask the minister to cross out that item 112 and make the amount equal in both cases.

When this matter was up before I pointed out that the minister was interfering perhaps in a way of which he was not aware, and I should like to bring the matter to his attention again to-night. I would say now that he is not acquainted with what this resolution means. It appears to-night as if the member who has just spoken considers the manufacturing end is the desiccated cocoanut.

No, I am going to point out another side. The minister has said that the cocoanut in the raw state is admitted free. There are certain companies in this country who take the raw cocoanut and shred it here, and by the proposed change you are taking the labour from the people of Canada and giving it to the cheap coloured labour in the southern islands; in a word you are putting the Canadian companies out of business. One is the Baker Company of Montreal. They are importing the cocoanut free and shredding it here. It is not a matter of sweetening the cocoanut; that is not the manufacturing condition. The shredding that the member has spoken about is done in the southern islands. It is the labour there that he is trying to protect. I am trying to protect the white labour in Canada against this proposed change. I repeat, the change now proposed by the minister will throw the shredding of the cocoanut back to the cheap coloured labour of the southern islands to the disadvantage of the white labour of Canada. When the member for East Calgary sees that point I hope he will change his attitude. The minister does not know what he is doing. I have a letter from the Baker people saying that they are thinking about closing up business because the preference on the shredded cocoanut is given to the cheap labour of the southern islands. The manufacturer, as I say, is shredding the raw cocoanut here. If this change goes through there will be no work for that class of labour in Canada. It is a small amount of labour, it is true, but it should be protected.

May I point out to my
hon. friend that these two articles do not deal with raw cocoanut, but simply with 78594-1484

And by the reduction you are simply throwing the labour back to the southern islands. It is not a case of sweetening, although it looks like it. Of course the cocoanut is sweetened afterwards, but that is not the crux of the case.

speechtext:
These reductions have been
generally well received, with the exception of the proposed tax on the transfer of stock. It has been represented to us that the proposed tax on mining shares was somewhat drastic, so I desire to move an amendment, as follows:
That paragraph 4 be amended by striking out clause (e) and substituting therefor the following:
(e)	one cent for every share of stock sold or transferred at a price over one dollar per share, but not more than three dollars per share:
(f)	one-fourth of one cent for every share of stock sold or transferred at a price over fifty cents per share, but not more than one dollar per share;
(g)	one-tenth of one cent for every share of stock sold or transferred at a price of fifty cents or less per share.
I think that will be fair.

I think the minister is still imposing too high a tax upon the cheaper shares. The effect of an unreasonable tax upon the lower priced shares will be to hinder the legitimate development of the mining industry and deprive the general public of an opportunity of sharing in the mining development which is now taking place in this country. The result will be that a monopoly will be placed in the hands of the larger interests. The fact that mining has developed to such an extent in British Columbia is due largely to the faith of the men with small savings, and if too high a tax is put upon these shares it will hinder legitimate mining development. The minister says that he is reducing the tax. He has reduced it very materially, but I should like to give a practical illustration of the effect of the tax as he had it compared with his present proposal. The Consolidated Mining & Smelting Company in British Columbia recently took over 74 per cent of the stock of the Caledonia mines on Vancouver island. They purchased outright 339,600 shares at 20 cents per share, a total value of $67,920. Under the minister's first proposal the tax would have been $3,396, or 5 per cent of the total price. On a purchase and sale the tax would have amounted to 10 per cent, or $6,792. A private investor could have purchased over $11,000,000 worth of securities of a par value of $100 and would have had to pay only the same amount of tax. The minister now proposes that the tax on shares worth 20 cents will be one-tenth of a cent. It is true that the tax is being reduced, but in my opinion it is still too high. Taking the illustration I have given, the tax would amount to $340 on a total purchase price of only $67,000, or over $700 on a purchase and sale of stock. I submit that that is too high; it is out of all proportion to the tax paid by the investor purchasing stocks on the
market. The legitimate mining development in British Columbia has been brought about by the smaller investors, the men with small savings guided by good engineers. In the case I have cited by way of illustration these men went out and prospected and they showed sufficient ore to interest the Consolidated Mining & Smelting Company. If the minister insists upon too high a tax upon the purchase and sale of these shares he will make them unmarketable and immediately kill tihe interest of the public in legitimate mining development. On shares sold or transferred at 50 cents the tax is to be one-quarter of one cent per share, or one-half cent per share on a purchase and sale. Let us consider the shares purchased by the Consolidated Mining & Smelting Company as being worth $1.01 per share. That would mean a purchase amounting to $342,996 worth of stock, and the minister proposes to put a tax of $3,396 upon that purchase. The same tax would permit of a purchase of over $11,000,000 worth of stock of a par value of $100, and I submit again that the proposed tax is out of all proportion and will discourage legitimate mining development in this country.

I had intended offering
some remarks in connection with this proposed amendment to part VII of the Special War Revenue Act, and the proposed reduction in the tax suggested by the hon. Minister of Finance this evening does not in any way change my view of the principle of the taxation; it merely offers, as a sop, a reduction in the burden cast upon the lower priced shares. To my mind this is most inequity able taxation. On the basis of the original proposal one buying or selling the lower priced issues would be paying a varying percentage in tax to the government. On one-cent shares the tax would be 100 per cent; on two-cent shares it would be 50 per cent; on three-cent shares the tax would amount to 33J per cent; on four-cent shares it would be 25 per cent, and so on down the list. I endeavoured to make a rapid calculation upon the proposed amendment, and as I figure it the purchaser will be paying 10 per cent tax on a one-cent share; 5 per cent tax on a two-cent share; 3.33 per cent tax on a three-cent share; 2.5 per cent tax on a four-cent share, and so on. In the case of the higher priced issues valued at $100, the percentage the purchaser will have to pay in the way of tax will amount to only 3/100 of one per cent. Let us consider for a moment the results of a tax of this nature, first, from the public standpoint, second, from the standpoint of the development of the
234S
Special War Revenue Act

mines, and third from the point of view of other far-reaching effects. The average speculator in mining stocks must of necessity speculate in the lower priced issues; it is only those of means who can interest themselves in the high priced issues. As I pointed out a moment ago, if a man sells stock at $100 a share he would be paying to the government 3/100 of one per cent of tthe sale price by way of tax, but if he sells stock at $1 a share he would be paying 1 per cent. This, to my mind, is iniquitous. It will, in my opinion, have an adverse effect in connection with the financing of the mines. I am not unmindful of the fact that, under the act as it stands, the original issue of treasury shares is not taxable, nor will it be under the amendment; but we must bear in mind the basis on which new mining properties are developed and the development financed. In the first place, companies are incorporated in order to get money, and money can be raised only in one of two ways: either you must engage a corps of salesmen who call upon individuals to sell them shares of stock, a method which is exceedingly expensive and which lends itself to all the possibilities of misrepresentation and fraud, or you must- offer that stock through some mining exchange where the divergence and width of the market make possible some fixed price. In order to offer that stock through an exchange, it is customary to have the issue underwritten by a broker or by some individual or corporation interested in the development of mining property. Obviously, for a new stock there is no demand which will produce funds to develop the property unless there is a market for the stock, and there will not be a demand unless the trading in that stock is active upon the market. Activity is obtained by brokers circularizing clients, by publishing the details of the property and its development to date in circulars, magazines, et cetera. The vast bulk of this class of stock consists of low priced issues; the moment you impose upon low priced issues a tax equal in percentage to the amounts indicated, you curtail trading in the market, and the moment you curtail trading in the market, you thereby prevent the company from obtaining the amount of funds which it would otherwise obtain for the development of those mines.
Let me cite a couple of concrete examples. Let us take Crown Reserve Consolidated, one of our mining issues, selling to-day at five cents. Under the original proposal there would be a tax of 20 per cent imposed on every sale. Under the new proposal there would be a tax

imposed of two per cent. It is not possible for that company to re-finance its operations and continue development with a tax at that rate imposed upon all the sales of its stock.
Let me take a more striking illustration, a new property in the Red Lake district. Picard a year ago was selling at 70 cents a share. To-day it is selling at approximately 3 cents a share. This is caused by the company running out of funds, being unable to sell more stock and having a bailiff come in to execute a judgment. That company is supposed to have .reasonable possibilities. It desires to re-finance. What opportunity has it of doing so when by this legislation you prevent an active market for those shares?
May I call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that many of the higher priced dividend paying stocks to-day, were a short time ago selling for 10 or 15 cents a share? A most striking example is Teck Hughes, which as late as 1921 was selling at 16 cents a share and which, I see by to-night's quotation, is listed at $9.60 a share. I took the record of the Standard Stock and Mining Exchange, because it is, I think, the largest mining exchange in Canada. If hon. members will look at the record they will find that there is a trading on that exchange now in 156 issues, of which 112, in other words, approximately 74 per cent, are stocks selling at under $3 a share. I endeavoured to make a computation of the difference the proposed tax would make on the basis of one day's trading. I admit I shall now have to revise it to some extent by reason of the amendment proposed to-night by the Minister of Finance, but I selected the tax paid in one day by eleven out of fifty brokers trading on the Standard' Stock and Mining Exchange. In one day broker No. 1 under the present basis of taxation would pay $190.29, and bear in mind that, in making that payment, he is merely the representative of the public who aa-e investing in stocks. Under the new rate of taxation he would pay, on stocks under $3, $5,901.50, and on stocks over $3, $78.75, or a total of $5,980.25 as against the $190.29 being paid to-day. Let me give you the totals of the computation of the eleven. In one day, on one exchange, eleven out of fifty brokers, who in turn would be charging to the customer the tax payable, would pay $21,037.89 in tax instead of $809.57.
Progress reported.
